items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like Coleman Hawkins. Like Bunny Berigan. Like Benny Goodman, Chu Berry, Dizzy Gillespie. They all had a sound that they could be recognized.

ctx.x: Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. Regardless what he played when he was there, you miss

seeing him. He had an aura about him that everybody loved. Everybody loved Count Basie. Everybody loved Duke Ellington. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. She’s the only one sounded like that. If Louis…
I guess it’s a tribute of a sort.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And I went out with Coleman Hawkins a lot of time, went to Toronto, Cleveland, I played with him, you know. We were good friends.

ctx.x: Yeah, he'd got enough income to float a while.

Sure. He was paying good salaries in those days, even when the bands were -- I know Johnny Hodges was making five, six hundred dollars a week when we were making $15.00 a night, you know. But it was really disappointing to me when Basie's band broke up. I didn't even know what I was going to do. And I went out with Coleman Hawkins a lot of time, went to Toronto, Cleveland, I played with him, you know. We were good friends.
And I just played with everybody around New York.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got a gig in Cleveland, come on get in the car, get your bag and make this week with me.

ctx.x: I didn’t have no plans, I just had a ball. I was having a good time. Because I was living on 122nd and 7th Avenue and that was right in the heart of everything. That’s a couple of blocks from Sugar Ray Robinson’s place, right around the corner from the Apollo, Theresa Hotel, there were so many places around there. And I had made so many friends that weren’t even in the

music business, they were just Basie fans. I’d be sitting out on the stoop in front of my building there, 2040 7th Avenue, somebody would say, “C’mon, Sweets, let’s go to the bar and have a taste,” you know, and I’d get up and I’d have a good time with them all night. Coleman Hawkins, he had come by and I remember the first time, I was sitting on the stoop and he said, “I got a gig in Cleveland, come on get in the car, get your bag and make this week with me.” I said, “Well, how much you going to pay, Bean?”,…
So, this was a little earlier.
